name: Quentin Talbert
languages: French (the school insisted, and the Army sent him to Orléans)
equipment: Heavy coat: a tan trench coat with a pen leaking slowly in the inside pocket
Walking stick: a blackthorn cane, since a knee that went wrong in the Army and has never gone right
Notebook and pencil, and a box of Bic pens
A press card: MILWAUKEE COURIER-LEDGER — STAFF
A list: eleven missing-persons reports from the wire morgue and the State Patrol, 1954 to 1973, all last placed in Kinnick County between September and October, with names, home towns and dates
Instant camera: a Polaroid SX-70 with three packs of film (30 pictures)
Tape recorder: a cassette recorder and a microphone on a cord
Newspaper: Sunday's Courier-Ledger with his byline on a story about a bus strike
A roll of dimes for payphones and a telephone card with his editor's home number
Car: a 1969 Plymouth Valiant, beige, with a typewriter on the back seat
features: Seen It in a Book (Educated origin: once per long rest he recalls one useful fact about history, science, law, geography or a book he has read without a check; advantage on Research checks in a library, archive or registry; he reads old handwriting and legal language without a check)

There's an Explanation (Skeptic: once per short rest, when he fails a fear check, he names a rational cause aloud, in character, and the failure becomes a success and he gains no Dread; if his explanation happens to be true, the GM tells him so. Advantage on Investigation checks to find the mechanism behind a thing that is not supernatural, and when he searches a room for 10 minutes the GM tells him without a check whether any part of what is happening in it is a person's doing)

Careful Notes (Skeptic: once per short rest, after 10 minutes examining a scene, he asks the GM 'What here has been moved?', 'Who was here most recently: a person, an animal or something else?' or 'What here does not fit?' and gets a true answer; it never names a creature's rule outright)

Calm Explanation (Skeptic, 2nd level: once per long rest, as an action, he explains a frightening phenomenon to allies who can hear him; until the end of the scene they have advantage on fear checks against that one phenomenon)

Discipline: Detective (Skeptic, 3rd level: advantage on Insight checks to tell whether a person is lying, and once per scenario a witness he has interviewed remembers one more true thing when he returns to them)

The Morgue and the Wire (Reporter background: he can get into any newspaper's back files and its staff will help him search them; he reads a court docket, a coroner's report and a police blotter; in any town with a paper he can find the person who knows the local gossip; a story with his name on it tells everyone involved who has been asking questions)

personality.traits: I believe in records, receipts and second sources. I am polite to everyone and trust nobody until I have checked. I hum Coltrane when I am thinking.
personality.ideals: Everybody who goes missing was somebody's. If nobody writes their name down, they vanish twice.
personality.bonds: My editor, Lou Pfeiffer, who gave me one week and fifty dollars. The eleven names on my list, whom I have never met and think about every night. My mother on Center Street in Milwaukee, who wants me to get married.
personality.flaws: I will explain away anything until I can't, and when I can't, I am going to be in real trouble, because I have no other way of holding on.

appearance: Thirty-four, a tall, slim Black man with a neat moustache, horn-rimmed glasses, a tan trench coat, a blackthorn cane he leans on more than he would like, and a Polaroid camera on a strap around his neck.
backstory: Quentin Talbert grew up on Milwaukee's North Side, the son of a Pullman porter and a schoolteacher, went to Marquette on a scholarship, was drafted in 1962 and spent two years as an Army clerk in France, where a jeep accident left him with the knee and the cane. He has been a reporter at the Milwaukee Courier-Ledger since 1965: city council, the 1967 open housing marches, courts, a bus strike. In August, writing a wire-service roundup on missing persons, he noticed a cluster: eleven reports in twenty years from all over the Midwest, a salesman, a hitchhiker, a hunter, a widower on a fishing trip, all last placed in one small county in western Wisconsin in September or October, all filed as adults who left of their own accord. His editor gave him a week and fifty dollars. He arrived in Hollow Fork on the Saturday Greyhound, and has noted already that it is the first small town in Wisconsin where nobody has stared at him; everyone has been perfectly, uniformly, unnervingly kind. (Hook: the story. His list is CLUE A1. He is the party's best researcher and the one most likely to put it on paper, or on television, in hs-scenario-004.)
